meta.title: fsc runtime knobs on top of the JIT flags
hardware: P-cluster L2 16 MB, E-cluster L2 4 MB, L1d 128 KB (P) / 64 KB (E), cache line 128 B
AC Power; Low Power Mode off
no thermal or CPU-power throttling warnings recorded (pmset -g therm)
method: Reference **base**: fsc from `main`, laid out like the SDK ships it (per-assembly ReadyToRun, Server GC), with `DOTNET_TieredPGO=0` and `DOTNET_TC_CallCountingDelayMs=0`, and parallel compilation on (the default).

Each other config changes one thing on top of base (see the table below). `ccd10` sets both JIT settings in `fsc.runtimeconfig.json` instead of env vars (equivalent; it avoids the hex parsing of env values).

fsc-level: the captured `FSharp.Compiler.Service.slnx` compilations, replayed in isolation: FCS net11.0, FSharp.Core netstandard2.0 (its first target framework) and FSharp.Build netstandard2.0 (small).

Whole build: `dotnet build fantomas.slnx -c Release --no-incremental` on SDK 11 RC1, with each config's fsc (`DotnetFscCompilerPath`) and settings applied to fsc processes only, through a wrapper. MSBuild keeps its defaults.
Runs per cell: 2–20, after 1 warm-up. Configs are interleaved in shuffled order every round. The warm-up also records the MultiCoreJit profile that the measured `mcj` runs use.
Host monitor and quiet-wait before every run, as in phases 1 and 2; disturbed runs are flagged, not dropped.

configs.desc: Reference: DOTNET_TieredPGO=0 + DOTNET_TC_CallCountingDelayMs=0 (env), parallel compilation on
Call-counting delay 10 ms instead of 0. Both JIT settings via fsc.runtimeconfig.json (System.Runtime.TieredPGO=false, CallCountingDelayMs=10), which avoids hex parsing of env values
+ DOTNET_gcConcurrent=0 (no background GC; the name is case-sensitive on macOS/Linux)
+ MultiCoreJit (ProfileOptimization) from a startup hook; one profile per compilation, recorded by the warm-up run
+ composite ReadyToRun image (crossgen2 --composite --inputbubble) of fsc, FSharp.Compiler.Service, FSharp.Core, FSharp.DependencyManager.Nuget

meta.flag_rule: foreign CPU > 1.0 core avg during the run, or host busy >= 1.0 core right before it, or any swapout, or > 5000 page compressions
meta.build_flag_rule: host busy >= 1.0 core right before the build, or any swapout (build CPU is system-wide, so foreign CPU is not separable)

findings_md:
## Summary (preliminary: quick pass)

These numbers come from the quick pass: 2 runs per config for FCS and Fantomas, 3 for FSharp.Core, 10 for FSharp.Build. The full pass (5 / 8 / 20 / 5 runs) replaces them when it finishes. Every change is relative to **base**: both JIT flags set and parallel compilation on.

### What helped

- **DATAS off** (`DOTNET_GCDynamicAdaptationMode=0`) is the only setting that is faster on every target, with lower CPU everywhere:
  - wall: FCS −4.5%, FSharp.Core −2.5%, FSharp.Build −11.3%, Fantomas build −2.6%
  - CPU: −7% to −18%
  - GC pause: −13% (FCS) to −83% (FSharp.Build)
  - Cost: peak memory goes up 37% (FCS) to 135% (FSharp.Core), because the GC no longer shrinks the heap.
- **Non-concurrent GC** (`DOTNET_gcConcurrent=0`): small wins. Wall changes by 0% to −3%, and CPU drops 4% to 9%. GC pause rises about 10%, but it costs less than the background GC it replaces.
- **4 GC heaps** (`DOTNET_GCHeapCount=4`, which also turns DATAS off) helps small compilations (FSharp.Build −11.8%) and saves CPU everywhere (−12% to −18%). It slows FCS by 7.8%, so it isn't a general win.
- **MultiCoreJit** makes no difference to wall time. It does cut Fantomas build CPU by 13%.

### What did not help

- **10 ms call-counting delay** instead of 0: slower on every target (+8% to +49% wall). It lowers CPU only for the small compilation (−25%). A delay of 0 is the right choice.
- **256 MB gen0 budget**: slower (+5% to +40% wall); GC pause goes up 30% to 233%.
- **Workstation GC**: much slower on large compilations (FCS +113% wall).
- **Composite ReadyToRun** of the compiler's own assemblies: slower (+3% to +14% wall). The image does load: without tiering, 39% fewer methods need JIT compilation at all. But more of the precompiled code becomes hot and is recompiled at tier 1, so total JIT work goes up.
- **Thread-pool minimum of 16 threads**: no effect.

### Next

- The full pass adds `datas_nonconc` (DATAS off plus non-concurrent GC). On FSharp.Build it is measured after the other configs instead of interleaved with them.
- These results are from one 11-core Apple M3 Pro. GC settings depend on core count and memory, so they need checking on the Linux x64 machines before recommending any.
